newsitem.title: USA: Versace killer still at large; Miami Beach on edge.
newsitem.headline: Versace killer still at large; Miami Beach on edge.

text.p: Police combed the Miami area on Wednesday night for the male prostitute and alleged serial killer suspected of murdering fashion king Gianni Versace.

But prime suspect Andrew Cunanan remained at large, leaving Miami Beach's gay community on edge. Police and FBI agents fanned out across the city, questioning people on the street, in gay bars, hotels, restaurants and nightclubs in the belief that Cunanan, already wanted in connection with four previous murders, might still be in the area.
Versace's body lay at the Riverside Gordon Memorial in north Miami Beach. Staff members were unable to give details of funeral arrangements.
A memorial service organised by the Italy-America Chamber of Commerce and city authorities is scheduled to be held on Friday at St.Patrick's Roman Catholic Church.
Versace's sister Donatella, a respected designer in her own right, visited her brother's mansion and left later in a limousine, witnesses said.

A crowd of admirers and curious onlookers stood all day outside the Spanish-style house on trendy Ocean Drive, leaving flowers, candles and notes on the steps where he slumped after a gunman pumped two shots into his head on Tuesday morning as he walked back from a cafe.
Police said they had received "very important" information in their manhunt for Cunanan.
"Unfortunately, what's taking place right now cannot be made public, because it's very sensitive," Miami Beach police spokesman Al Boza told reporters.
TV Channel 6 said Cunanan was reported to have been sighted in a bar in Boca Raton called Choices, but Boza told Reuters he had no knowledge of that.
"They're generating their own tips. ... It's beginning to get a bit silly," he said.
FBI Special Agent Paul Philip said the hunt was concentrating on the Miami area. "It's quite possible he might be holed up someplace," he said.
But Boza said Cunanan's whereabouts were still not known and he could have fled the state.
Cunanan, 27, was already on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list, sought in connection with four murders during a killing spree in northern U.S. states in April and May.

He is the only suspect in the execution-style slaying of the Italian designer, who had revolutionised the fashion world and dressed the world's beautiful people, including Princess Diana; singers Madonna, Sting and Elton John; and actresses Demi Moore and Liz Hurley.
As police combed South Beach bars and hotels for the suspect, gays said they feared he was still in their midst.
Danilo de la Torre, an actor who performs as a drag queen in South Beach clubs, said his show was nearly empty on Tuesday night as customers stayed home to watch news about the murder.
"People are shocked it could happen, really shocked and scared. He's still out there," de la Torre said.
Carl Weersing, 36, said the gay community wondered if the killer had spent some time stalking Versace and whether other gay men were in danger.
"I'm being really careful," Weersing said outside Club Body Tech, a gym frequented by male homosexual weightlifters.
"I know last night friends of mine who were out walking their dogs, and they said, 'We're walking in pairs.' It really puts a whole new consciousness on the situation," Weersing said.
Police said they did not know if Versace, a homosexual, had any relationship with Cunanan.
Weersing said while Versace was not a flamboyant member of the community, he frequented gay hangouts.
Vanity Fair magazine said Versace knew Cunanan.
A profile of Cunanan to appear in its September issue reported an exchange between the two men at the San Francisco Opera.
In a release from the magazine, a friend of Cunanan is quoted as saying Versace recognised Cunanan backstage.
"I remember you. Lago de Como, no?" the friend quoted Versace as saying to Cunanan.
The article said that "for Cunanan, who craved attention and for whom namedropping was second nature, these were moments he lived for."
The magazine released details of the profile by Maureen Orth after the slaying, but it did not say when the exchange took place or give more details about their relationship.
Orth said Cunanan, 27, had a number of wealthy patrons and targeted the people he wanted to meet.
"He would investigate older, wealthy gay men who didn't have families, and he would place himself in those circles, and that was his living," a friend told Vanity Fair.
